titles: Supporting data for publication: Environmental impact of upstream processing strategies for E. coli-based antibody fragment production
descriptions:
Context and methodology

This dataset contains research data underlying the publication “Environmental impact of upstream processing strategies for E. coli-based antibody fragment production: green metrics versus life cycle assessment”.

The study investigates the environmental impact of different upstream processing strategies for microbial production of the fragment antigen-binding (Fab) ranibizumab using Escherichia coli. Four bioreactor operation strategies were compared: fed-batch (FB), repetitive fed-batch (RFB), Chemostat cultivation, and a cascaded continuous setup.

The purpose of the dataset is to provide the underlying experimental and calculated data used for the sustainability assessment presented in the publication. The assessment combines process-based green metrics, namely process mass intensity (PMI), manufacturing mass intensity (MMI), and energetic footprint (EF), with a cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment (LCA). The LCA considers global warming potential (GWP) and water consumption footprint (WF).

Material consumption data were derived from the experimentally performed laboratory-scale cultivation processes and associated upstream unit operations. Electrical energy consumption of laboratory equipment was experimentally monitored where applicable. Additional energy demands, including purified-water production and conditioning as well as scale-dependent aeration and stirring scenarios, were calculated using literature data and process assumptions. LCA calculations were performed using SimaPro 9.6.0.1 with the ecoinvent 3.10 database and the ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint (H) impact assessment method. The functional unit of the sustainability assessment was 1 g of produced Fab.

Sensitivity and scenario analyses include variations in product titer (±20%), electricity supply mix, and scale-dependent stirring energy demand.

Technical details

The dataset consists of three Microsoft Excel workbooks:

PMI_MMI_data.xlsx contains the material input data and calculations used to determine PMI and MMI for the four upstream processing configurations. Data are provided by material category and unit operation, together with the corresponding product-normalized results and sensitivity calculations.

Energy_data.xlsx contains experimentally measured electrical energy data and calculated energy demands used to determine the energetic footprint (EF). Separate worksheets contain data for sterilization-in-place (SIP), pre-culture/incubation, bioreactor operation, centrifugation, purified-water production and conditioning, and aeration/stirring calculations. The summary_data worksheet combines these contributions and reports absolute and product-specific energy demands for the four process configurations.

LCA_data.xlsx contains the resulting life-cycle-assessment data for global warming potential and water consumption footprint, including contributions from individual process and material categories. The workbook additionally contains the data used for the scenario and sensitivity analyses.

The files can be opened with Microsoft Excel or compatible spreadsheet software. No specialized software is required to inspect the deposited data. Reproduction of the original LCA modelling from the underlying life-cycle inventory databases requires access to SimaPro and the corresponding ecoinvent database.

Further details

The four process configurations are abbreviated as FB (fed-batch), RFB (repetitive fed-batch), Chemostat, and Cascaded setup. Additional abbreviations used throughout the dataset include PMI (process mass intensity), MMI (manufacturing mass intensity), EF (energetic footprint), GWP (global warming potential), WF (water consumption footprint), SIP (sterilization-in-place), CIP (cleaning-in-place), PW (purified water), and Fab (fragment antigen-binding).

The system boundaries, process assumptions, experimental procedures, calculation methodology, and interpretation of the data are described in detail in the associated publication. The deposited spreadsheets contain both primary experimental measurements and derived/calculated values.

descriptions: The Texas Natural History Collections (TNHC) are administratively part of the Biodiversity Center, in the Department of Integrative Biology of the University of Texas (UT Austin). The Ichthyology Collection (TNHCi, formerly TNHC) includes over 70,000 lots that contain over 1,500,000 specimens. Most of those are “wet” collections, with specimens initially fixed in 10% formalin and permanently stored in 70% ethanol. The oldest specimens were collected in 1912 but a very strong peak in collection activity in Texas from 1950–1980 reflects the work of Dr. Clark Hubbs and his lab. More recently, collections by Dean Hendrickson’s lab and a diversity of collectors from UT Austin and other Texas academic institutions, as well as state and federal agencies (Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD), Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ), United States Geological Survey (USGS)) continue to contribute to growth, as does the Hendrickson Lab’s Fishes of Texas Project (www.fishesoftexas.org), primarily funded by TPWD. We have a small collection of larval fishes (in 10% formalin) from Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands, and an osteological collection with 800 cleared and stained specimens (including all Texas species) and 500 dry skeletons. Many of the skeletal specimens originate from W. W. Dalquest (Midwestern University) and his students. Our >2,000 tissue samples in vials with 100% ethanol are stored in liquid nitrogen in the Biodiversity Center’s Genetic Resources Collection. Most are linked to whole preserved specimens. Our type specimens include 3 holotypes, 116 paratypes, and 1 allotype. Collections acquired from other institutions include that of the University of Texas at Austin’s Marine Science Institute (>3,000 lots, acquired in 1990), Midwestern University (2000, >1,400 lots), Texas Tech University (>1,300 lots, 2000), Texas A&M University Kingsville (>5,200 lots), University of Texas at Brownsville (>1,100 lots) and Lamar University (~1,200 lots), Northeastern Louisiana University Monroe (2,084 lots). Large accessions remaining to be cataloged include (but are not limited to) collections provided by Dr. Robert Edwards (state-wide with focus on Rio Grande and coast), Dr. Tim Bonner (State-wide, with focus on Brazos), Matthew Acre (~1,800 larval specimens from the Trinity River), TPWD (state-wide), Seiji Miyazono (Pecos), Bill Birkhead (Mexico), and TCEQ (state-wide).

descriptions: Synthetic Sdiff splitting measurements and AxiSEM3D waveforms for 51 elastic tensors and three layer thicknesses. The 153 model configurations each contain 96 measurements spanning four epicentral distances and 24 propagation azimuths, giving 14,688 records in total. The measurement archive includes the MATLAB results and SplitRacer diagnostic plots. The waveform archive contains the simulation inputs and outputs. Processing and analysis code is available in the companion software deposit, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19673399.

titles: MALT-OMEGA Stage 4 Technical Disclosure: Multi-Grid Fokker-Planck Time-Domain Verification, Non-Maxwellian Slow-Electron Depletion, Centrifugal-Ambipolar Stratification, and the 8.275 T Zero-Trim Equilibrium / 8.350 T Ignition Bifurcation in a High-Beta p-11B Linear Magnetic Mirror
descriptions:
This disclosure presents the Stage 4 mathematical and computational verification of the MALT-OMEGA continuous-flow proton-boron-11 (p-11B) linear magnetic mirror fusion architecture. Previous zero-dimensional (0D) homogeneous plasma models assuming static Maxwellian electron distributions inevitably quench under Spitzer electron drag (Rider, 1995) or suffer unphysical beam energy runaway when auxiliary heating is modeled as a scalar variable. To eliminate all static assumptions and planted multipliers, this update replaces 0D scalar approximations with a coupled 4-Grid Finite-Difference Time-Domain (FDTD) and Fokker-Planck Multi-Physics Simulator stepping at 2.5 ms resolution across four coupled physical domains:





Grid 1 (120-Bin Fast-Proton Fokker-Planck Energy PDE): Solves the time-dependent advection-diffusion distribution f_f(E, t) across E in [15 keV, 900 keV]. Neutral beam protons are injected at the 597.4 keV (1.07 x 10^7 m/s) Sikora-Weller (2016) resonance peak (548 keV center-of-mass) and supported against collisional slowing-down by quasilinear radiofrequency (RF) alpha channeling locked to the fundamental proton / second-harmonic alpha cyclotron resonance (1 * Omega_p = 2 * Omega_alpha). Relativistic and Doppler resonance windowing naturally bounds fast-proton acceleration below 640 keV, preventing unphysical beam runaway while sustaining a hybrid fast-ion and thermal-ion burn (Kolmes, Ochs, & Fisch, 2022-2024).




Grid 2 (200-Node Rosenbluth Velocity-Space Drag & 2.5 Hz Breathing-Lung Thermal Separation): By the Rosenbluth-MacDonald-Judd (1957) Fokker-Planck shell theorem, net dynamical friction on a 597.4 keV proton is exerted exclusively by slow electrons with velocities v_e <= v_p, corresponding to a kinetic energy cutoff of E_e <= (m_e / m_p) * E_p = 325.4 eV (representing only 0.039% of a 50 keV Maxwellian electron bulk). MALT-OMEGA utilizes a synchronized 2.5 Hz electrostatic capacitor end-plug and ECH/laser thermal barrier cycle ("Breathing Lung") to selectively evacuate this sub-325.4 eV electron pocket while flushing cooled He-4 alpha ash (< 0.88% steady-state concentration; Ochs, Kolmes, & Fisch, 2025). The solver explicitly penalizes net electrical output by subtracting the continuous recirculating power required to maintain the depleted slow-electron cavity against electron-electron collisional refill (Physics of Plasmas 32, 012101, 2025).




Grid 3 (100-Node Radial Centrifugal-Ambipolar Stratification & 10-Pole Decapole Boundary): Solves the coupled Poisson-Boltzmann-centrifugal quasineutrality equations for rotating multi-species mirror plasmas (Kolmes, Ochs, & Fisch, Physical Review Letters 136, 085102, 2026). Azimuthal E x B rotation concentrates heavy 11B(5+) ions into an outer radial reaction shell (+34.2% effective target density across 0.50 <= r/a <= 0.92), while the resulting ambipolar electric field pushes thermal background protons inward ("inverted centrifugal confinement"), reducing orbit-averaged electron drag density along the fast-proton path to 82% of the bulk average. Core MHD flute stability and synchrotron suppression are maintained by a 10-pole (decapole) magnetic boundary (B_wall proportional to r^4), golden-ratio (phi = 1.618) aperiodic axial coil spacing driving Aubry-Andre-Harper wave localization (arXiv:2604.08321), and a 5.51-Ohm Saturn-type auroral exhaust load matching the torsional Alfven wave impedance (reflection coefficient Gamma_Alfven -> 0.032).




Grid 4 (60-Node 1D Radial First-Wall Thermal PDE & Gridless Adiabatic Drift DEC): Enforces strict First-Law thermodynamic partitioning across a 4.50 m^3 core (16.0 m^2 first-wall surface area). All Bremsstrahlung X-ray power is routed through a 60-node transient heat conduction solver modeling the 4-layer first wall (flowing liquid FLiBe curtain, SiC manifold, BN:H / HfO2 dielectric thermal barrier, and cascaded SiGe thermoelectric / sCO2 recovery loop operating at 42% thermal efficiency below the 450 C hot-junction limit and 2.80 MW/m^2 flux ceiling). Charged plasma exhaust exits through an Arefiev-Breizman (2008) supersonic ambipolar magnetic nozzle—which converts electron thermal pressure into directed axial ion kinetic energy—directly into a Rax, Kolmes, & Fisch (PRX Energy 4, 013007, 2025) gridless adiabatic grad-B and curvature drift Direct Energy Converter operating at 81% electrical recovery efficiency without inline grid sputtering.



DYNAMIC MAGNETIC TRIMMING & THE 3-TIER SCALING / IGNITION CLIFF DISCOVERY:

To prevent high-beta diamagnetic drift from detuning the 1 * Omega_p = 2 * Omega_alpha cyclotron resonance lock (B_int = B_ext * sqrt(1 - beta) at design beta = 0.360), MALT-OMEGA pairs its primary high-temperature superconducting REBCO coils with an active low-inductance coated copper trimming coil (dB_Cu limited to +/- 2.00 T) and demand-throttled neutral beam injection. Parametric time-domain sweeps across magnetic field strengths within the fixed 4.50 m^3 vessel revealed a sharp thermodynamic bifurcation ("The Ignition Cliff") separating passively safe beam-sustained amplifiers from thermally ignited cores:





Tier 1 Pilot Demonstrator (Option B: 5.00 T REBCO Base / 4.000 T Internal Lock at 60.98 MHz): Operates at n_p = 0.617 x 10^20 m^-3 in a passively safe, sub-ignited regime. Bulk ion temperature settles to T_i = 72.1 keV and electron temperature to T_e = 36.5 keV, requiring a minor negative copper trim of dB_Cu = -0.167 T. Produces 2.67 MW_th fusion power and +1.71 MWe net electricity to the grid (Q_eng = +3.60) with a first-wall heat flux of 0.07 MW/m^2 (40x below the 2.80 MW/m^2 limit) and 106.3 MPa coil hoop stress (6.3x below the 700 MPa REBCO limit).




Tier 2 Commercial Modular Unit (Option C: 7.75 T REBCO Base / 6.200 T Internal Lock at 94.52 MHz): Operates at n_p = 1.481 x 10^20 m^-3 with walk-away passive safety. Equilibrium settles at T_i = 81.7 keV, T_e = 40.3 keV, and <E_f> = 653.9 keV with a copper trim excursion of only dB_Cu = -0.187 T (9.4% of trim capacity). Produces 15.07 MW_th fusion power and +9.52 MWe net electricity (Q_eng = +3.47) at 0.43 MW/m^2 wall heat flux (15.4% of material limit), 388.6 C SiGe hot-junction temperature, and 250.8 MPa magnet hoop stress (35.8% of structural limit).




The Zero-Trim Equilibrium Point (8.275 T REBCO Base / 6.620 T Internal Lock at 100.92 MHz): High-resolution FDTD sweeps between 8.25 T (dB_Cu = -0.044 T, +14.43 MWe) and 8.30 T (dB_Cu = +0.046 T, +16.27 MWe) isolate the exact zero-trim equilibrium point at B_REBCO = 8.275 T. At this field, alpha-particle bulk ion heating exactly balances conductive transport losses at T_i = 98.0 keV and T_e = 43.5 keV, allowing the copper trimming coil to rest at dB_Cu = 0.000 T while delivering ~15.50 MWe net electrical power at a safe 0.61 MW/m^2 wall flux.




The Ignition Cliff & Utility-Scale Core (8.350 T Threshold to Option A at 10.50 T REBCO Base): Increasing the base field across the 8.350 T threshold (dB_Cu = +0.684 T, +29.93 MWe) to 8.400 T triggers a self-heating hybrid fast-thermal ignition bifurcation. At Option A (10.50 T REBCO Base / 8.400 T Target, 128.06 MHz, n_p = 2.719 x 10^20 m^-3), bulk ion temperature self-heats to 350.0 keV, driving fusion power to 155.57 MW_th and net electrical output to +108.81 MWe (Q_eng = +5.27). However, inside a compact 4.50 m^3 vessel, this ignition surge saturates the +2.000 T copper trim ceiling and pushes wall heat flux to 3.36 MW/m^2 (120% of the 2.80 MW/m^2 limit). This mathematically bounds the compact 4.50 m^3 vessel to the 5.00 T - 8.275 T commercial window, while proving that utility-scale (> 100 MWe) ignited cores above 8.35 T simply require scaling the first-wall surface area from 16.0 m^2 to ~32.0 m^2.

descriptions:
This disclosure presents the Stage 4 mathematical and computational verification of the MALT-OMEGA continuous-flow proton-boron-11 (p-11B) linear magnetic mirror fusion architecture. Previous zero-dimensional (0D) homogeneous plasma models assuming static Maxwellian electron distributions inevitably quench under Spitzer electron drag (Rider, 1995) or suffer unphysical beam energy runaway when auxiliary heating is modeled as a scalar variable. To eliminate all static assumptions and planted multipliers, this update replaces 0D scalar approximations with a coupled 4-Grid Finite-Difference Time-Domain (FDTD) and Fokker-Planck Multi-Physics Simulator stepping at 2.5 ms resolution across four coupled physical domains:





Grid 1 (120-Bin Fast-Proton Fokker-Planck Energy PDE): Solves the time-dependent advection-diffusion distribution f_f(E, t) across E in [15 keV, 900 keV]. Neutral beam protons are injected at the 597.4 keV (1.07 x 10^7 m/s) Sikora-Weller (2016) resonance peak (548 keV center-of-mass) and supported against collisional slowing-down by quasilinear radiofrequency (RF) alpha channeling locked to the fundamental proton / second-harmonic alpha cyclotron resonance (1 * Omega_p = 2 * Omega_alpha). Relativistic and Doppler resonance windowing naturally bounds fast-proton acceleration below 640 keV, preventing unphysical beam runaway while sustaining a hybrid fast-ion and thermal-ion burn (Kolmes, Ochs, & Fisch, 2022-2024).




Grid 2 (200-Node Rosenbluth Velocity-Space Drag & 2.5 Hz Breathing-Lung Thermal Separation): By the Rosenbluth-MacDonald-Judd (1957) Fokker-Planck shell theorem, net dynamical friction on a 597.4 keV proton is exerted exclusively by slow electrons with velocities v_e <= v_p, corresponding to a kinetic energy cutoff of E_e <= (m_e / m_p) * E_p = 325.4 eV (representing only 0.039% of a 50 keV Maxwellian electron bulk). MALT-OMEGA utilizes a synchronized 2.5 Hz electrostatic capacitor end-plug and ECH/laser thermal barrier cycle ("Breathing Lung") to selectively evacuate this sub-325.4 eV electron pocket while flushing cooled He-4 alpha ash (< 0.88% steady-state concentration; Ochs, Kolmes, & Fisch, 2025). The solver explicitly penalizes net electrical output by subtracting the continuous recirculating power required to maintain the depleted slow-electron cavity against electron-electron collisional refill (Physics of Plasmas 32, 012101, 2025).




Grid 3 (100-Node Radial Centrifugal-Ambipolar Stratification & 10-Pole Decapole Boundary): Solves the coupled Poisson-Boltzmann-centrifugal quasineutrality equations for rotating multi-species mirror plasmas (Kolmes, Ochs, & Fisch, Physical Review Letters 136, 085102, 2026). Azimuthal E x B rotation concentrates heavy 11B(5+) ions into an outer radial reaction shell (+34.2% effective target density across 0.50 <= r/a <= 0.92), while the resulting ambipolar electric field pushes thermal background protons inward ("inverted centrifugal confinement"), reducing orbit-averaged electron drag density along the fast-proton path to 82% of the bulk average. Core MHD flute stability and synchrotron suppression are maintained by a 10-pole (decapole) magnetic boundary (B_wall proportional to r^4), golden-ratio (phi = 1.618) aperiodic axial coil spacing driving Aubry-Andre-Harper wave localization (arXiv:2604.08321), and a 5.51-Ohm Saturn-type auroral exhaust load matching the torsional Alfven wave impedance (reflection coefficient Gamma_Alfven -> 0.032).




Grid 4 (60-Node 1D Radial First-Wall Thermal PDE & Gridless Adiabatic Drift DEC): Enforces strict First-Law thermodynamic partitioning across a 4.50 m^3 core (16.0 m^2 first-wall surface area). All Bremsstrahlung X-ray power is routed through a 60-node transient heat conduction solver modeling the 4-layer first wall (flowing liquid FLiBe curtain, SiC manifold, BN:H / HfO2 dielectric thermal barrier, and cascaded SiGe thermoelectric / sCO2 recovery loop operating at 42% thermal efficiency below the 450 C hot-junction limit and 2.80 MW/m^2 flux ceiling). Charged plasma exhaust exits through an Arefiev-Breizman (2008) supersonic ambipolar magnetic nozzle—which converts electron thermal pressure into directed axial ion kinetic energy—directly into a Rax, Kolmes, & Fisch (PRX Energy 4, 013007, 2025) gridless adiabatic grad-B and curvature drift Direct Energy Converter operating at 81% electrical recovery efficiency without inline grid sputtering.



DYNAMIC MAGNETIC TRIMMING & THE 3-TIER SCALING / IGNITION CLIFF DISCOVERY:

To prevent high-beta diamagnetic drift from detuning the 1 * Omega_p = 2 * Omega_alpha cyclotron resonance lock (B_int = B_ext * sqrt(1 - beta) at design beta = 0.360), MALT-OMEGA pairs its primary high-temperature superconducting REBCO coils with an active low-inductance coated copper trimming coil (dB_Cu limited to +/- 2.00 T) and demand-throttled neutral beam injection. Parametric time-domain sweeps across magnetic field strengths within the fixed 4.50 m^3 vessel revealed a sharp thermodynamic bifurcation ("The Ignition Cliff") separating passively safe beam-sustained amplifiers from thermally ignited cores:





Tier 1 Pilot Demonstrator (Option B: 5.00 T REBCO Base / 4.000 T Internal Lock at 60.98 MHz): Operates at n_p = 0.617 x 10^20 m^-3 in a passively safe, sub-ignited regime. Bulk ion temperature settles to T_i = 72.1 keV and electron temperature to T_e = 36.5 keV, requiring a minor negative copper trim of dB_Cu = -0.167 T. Produces 2.67 MW_th fusion power and +1.71 MWe net electricity to the grid (Q_eng = +3.60) with a first-wall heat flux of 0.07 MW/m^2 (40x below the 2.80 MW/m^2 limit) and 106.3 MPa coil hoop stress (6.3x below the 700 MPa REBCO limit).




Tier 2 Commercial Modular Unit (Option C: 7.75 T REBCO Base / 6.200 T Internal Lock at 94.52 MHz): Operates at n_p = 1.481 x 10^20 m^-3 with walk-away passive safety. Equilibrium settles at T_i = 81.7 keV, T_e = 40.3 keV, and <E_f> = 653.9 keV with a copper trim excursion of only dB_Cu = -0.187 T (9.4% of trim capacity). Produces 15.07 MW_th fusion power and +9.52 MWe net electricity (Q_eng = +3.47) at 0.43 MW/m^2 wall heat flux (15.4% of material limit), 388.6 C SiGe hot-junction temperature, and 250.8 MPa magnet hoop stress (35.8% of structural limit).




The Zero-Trim Equilibrium Point (8.275 T REBCO Base / 6.620 T Internal Lock at 100.92 MHz): High-resolution FDTD sweeps between 8.25 T (dB_Cu = -0.044 T, +14.43 MWe) and 8.30 T (dB_Cu = +0.046 T, +16.27 MWe) isolate the exact zero-trim equilibrium point at B_REBCO = 8.275 T. However, inside a compact 4.50 m^3 vessel, this ignition surge saturates the +2.000 T copper trim ceiling and pushes wall heat flux to 3.36 MW/m^2 (120% of the 2.80 MW/m^2 limit). This mathematically bounds the compact 4.50 m^3 vessel to the 5.00 T - 8.275 T commercial window, while proving that utility-scale (> 100 MWe) ignited cores above 8.35 T simply require scaling the first-wall surface area from 16.0 m^2 to ~32.0 m^2.

descriptions:
This dataset is the supplementary material for the manuscript "Decision Neutrality of Forecast Revisions in Microgrids with Photovoltaics and Battery Storage" by Yun Xing (Hohai University), submitted to Applied Sciences (MDPI). Version 1.0, 25 October 2026.

OverviewThe study asks when adopting a revised next-day forecast changes a battery dispatch decision, rather than only the predicted cost. It derives two checkable sufficient reset conditions under which old and revised forecasts produce next-day storage value functions that differ only by an additive constant. A fixed-input perturbation bound separates this local neutrality from realized rolling-policy performance. Five policies (FF, FS, SF, SS and DAY) are compared on 522 community-days from 270 measured households aggregated into nine synthetic communities, with three synthetic tariffs and two import regimes.

Key results- Freezing next-day forecasts is numerically neutral under unlimited imports across the tested tariffs.- Under a 30 kW import cap and time-of-use pricing, retaining midnight targets (DAY) lowers total operating cost by 3.105% relative to full updating (FF). Lower unmet-demand penalties account for 88.3% of the reduction; the import-bill reduction is 0.588%.- Freezing both forecasts while replanning (SS) costs 0.054% more than FF under the same six-hour replanning schedule, separating forecast adoption from target retention.- Under the same cap and tariff, freezing only the next-day forecast (FS) costs 0.188% more than FF.- Matched-calendar comparisons show that the magnitude of update effects depends on the controller scheme.

Contents1. Supporting_Results_and_Protocol.zip: verified reproducibility archive with 3,833 files, including fixed protocols, derived community inputs, customer-community mapping, analysis code, result tables, 15,660 policy-day records, 9,396 local terminal comparisons, 1,496 matched-calendar controller records, half-hour trajectories, figures and an internal manifest.2. Supplementary_Guide.pdf: Supplementary Methods S1 and S2, extended uncertainty tables S1-S6, data dictionary notes and the run sequence.3. README_ZENODO.txt: contents, usage order and scope notes.4. LICENSE.txt: licensing note for code and derived data.5. CITATION.cff: citation metadata.6. zenodo_metadata.json: suggested metadata for this record.7. SHA256SUMS.txt: SHA-256 checksums of the files in this archive.

The recorded environment is Python 3.13.9 with NumPy 2.3.5, SciPy 1.16.3, pandas 2.3.3, Matplotlib 3.10.6 and openpyxl 3.1.5. Entry points cover the primary experiment, aggregation, availability sensitivity, diagnostics, both controller families, benchmarks and independent checks. The archive also supports a fresh single-group replay and a full audit without the author's original workspace.

descriptions:
A synthetic dataset of 500 long multi-turn Arabic conversations with a mean conversation length of 33.056 turns, median of 33 turns, range of 24–48 turns, and a total of 16,528 turns (where every turn is one user message together with its expected agent response).

Conversation length in tokens has a mean of 9,901, a median of 11,060, and a range of 710–18,456. Token counts cover the user side of each conversation and are computed under the cl100k_base tokenizer, since the dataset specifies an expected response for each turn rather than a fixed agent reply.

The dataset is not partitioned. It is intended for evaluation rather than training, so all 500 conversations form a single test set.

Each conversation follows one of five composition templates, allocated in equal proportion at 100 conversations each, combining personal information about a fictional persona with excerpts from Arabic Wikipedia articles and short general-knowledge exchanges. Every turn is annotated with the memory-dependent design objectives it probes, an English description of its role in the conversation, and the expected response. Across the dataset this yields 22,214 objective instances over ten design objectives, of which 16,310 query information established earlier in the same conversation. The number of turns separating a queried fact from its introduction has a median of 15 and a maximum of 47.

The generation process drew on 1,200 Arabic Wikipedia articles spanning thirteen categories and totalling 4,649,321 words, with each article used in exactly one conversation, and on a curated pool of 1,244 Arabic general-knowledge topics across seventeen categories. Conversations were produced with Gemma 3 (12B) under a fixed random seed, from a plan computed deterministically in advance.

Article content is derived from Arabic Wikipedia (https://ar.wikipedia.org), licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-SA 4.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/). Articles were modified by extracting contiguous runs of whole sections of roughly 2,000 to 6,000 characters. In accordance with the ShareAlike term, this dataset is released under CC BY-SA 4.0.

titles: Open Intelligence Quantization Benchmark Dataset: Test Prompts and Raw Latency Measurements
descriptions:
Supplementary data for the paper "Open Intelligence: A CPU-Only Multimodal LLM Serving System and an Empirical Study  of GGUF Quantization."

  This dataset contains:  1. 100 custom visual question-answering prompts used to benchmark 6 GGUF quantization formats (Q2_K through Q8_0)  2. Raw latency measurements for all 600 inferences (100 prompts × 6 models)

  Key findings: Q3_K_S achieves optimal CPU inference performance (11.06s p50 latency, 100% success rate) despite being  smaller than Q4-Q8 formats, demonstrating non-monotonic quantization behavior on memory-bandwidth-bound hardware.

  Hardware: Linode Dedicated 16GB (Intel Xeon E5-2680 v4, 4 vCPUs, 16GB RAM)  Runtime: llama-cpp-python v0.2.79, AVX2-enabled, sequential execution  Configuration: Temperature 0.3, 150 max tokens, 4096 context size

  Files included:  - quantization_benchmark_prompts.md (10KB): Complete prompt list with benchmark configuration, performance summary,  and reproducibility notes  - quantization_raw_latencies.csv (104KB): All 600 raw latency measurements with per-prompt, per-model data

titles: Arabic Long-Context Conversational Memory Dataset
institutions: Arab Academy for Science, Technology, and Maritime Transport
descriptions:
A synthetic dataset of 500 long multi-turn Arabic conversations with a mean conversation length of 33.056 turns, median of 33 turns, range of 24–48 turns, and a total of 16,528 turns (where every turn is one user message together with its expected agent response).

Conversation length in tokens has a mean of 9,901, a median of 11,060, and a range of 710–18,456. Token counts cover the user side of each conversation and are computed under the cl100k_base tokenizer, since the dataset specifies an expected response for each turn rather than a fixed agent reply.

The dataset is not partitioned. It is intended for evaluation rather than training, so all 500 conversations form a single test set.

Each conversation follows one of five composition templates, allocated in equal proportion at 100 conversations each, combining personal information about a fictional persona with excerpts from Arabic Wikipedia articles and short general-knowledge exchanges. Every turn is annotated with the memory-dependent design objectives it probes, an English description of its role in the conversation, and the expected response. Across the dataset this yields 22,214 objective instances over ten design objectives, of which 16,310 query information established earlier in the same conversation. The number of turns separating a queried fact from its introduction has a median of 15 and a maximum of 47.

The generation process drew on 1,200 Arabic Wikipedia articles spanning thirteen categories and totalling 4,649,321 words, with each article used in exactly one conversation, and on a curated pool of 1,244 Arabic general-knowledge topics across seventeen categories. Conversations were produced with Gemma 3 (12B) under a fixed random seed, from a plan computed deterministically in advance.

Article content is derived from Arabic Wikipedia (https://ar.wikipedia.org), licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-SA 4.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/). Articles were modified by extracting contiguous runs of whole sections of roughly 2,000 to 6,000 characters. In accordance with the ShareAlike term, this dataset is released under CC BY-SA 4.0.

descriptions: The Texas Natural History Collections (TNHC) are administratively part of the Biodiversity Center, in the Department of Integrative Biology of the University of Texas (UT Austin). The Ichthyology Collection (TNHCi, formerly TNHC) includes over 70,000 lots that contain over 1,500,000 specimens. Most of those are “wet” collections, with specimens initially fixed in 10% formalin and permanently stored in 70% ethanol. The oldest specimens were collected in 1912 but a very strong peak in collection activity in Texas from 1950–1980 reflects the work of Dr. Clark Hubbs and his lab. More recently, collections by Dean Hendrickson’s lab and a diversity of collectors from UT Austin and other Texas academic institutions, as well as state and federal agencies (Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD), Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ), United States Geological Survey (USGS)) continue to contribute to growth, as does the Hendrickson Lab’s Fishes of Texas Project (www.fishesoftexas.org), primarily funded by TPWD. We have a small collection of larval fishes (in 10% formalin) from Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands, and an osteological collection with 800 cleared and stained specimens (including all Texas species) and 500 dry skeletons. Many of the skeletal specimens originate from W. W. Dalquest (Midwestern University) and his students. Our >2,000 tissue samples in vials with 100% ethanol are stored in liquid nitrogen in the Biodiversity Center’s Genetic Resources Collection. Most are linked to whole preserved specimens. Our type specimens include 3 holotypes, 116 paratypes, and 1 allotype. Collections acquired from other institutions include that of the University of Texas at Austin’s Marine Science Institute (>3,000 lots, acquired in 1990), Midwestern University (2000, >1,400 lots), Texas Tech University (>1,300 lots, 2000), Texas A&M University Kingsville (>5,200 lots), University of Texas at Brownsville (>1,100 lots) and Lamar University (~1,200 lots), Northeastern Louisiana University Monroe (2,084 lots). Large accessions remaining to be cataloged include (but are not limited to) collections provided by Dr. Robert Edwards (state-wide with focus on Rio Grande and coast), Dr. Tim Bonner (State-wide, with focus on Brazos), Matthew Acre (~1,800 larval specimens from the Trinity River), TPWD (state-wide), Seiji Miyazono (Pecos), Bill Birkhead (Mexico), and TCEQ (state-wide).

titles: Supporting data for publication: Environmental impact of upstream processing strategies for E. coli-based antibody fragment production
descriptions:
Context and methodology

This dataset contains research data underlying the publication “Environmental impact of upstream processing strategies for E. coli-based antibody fragment production: green metrics versus life cycle assessment”.

The study investigates the environmental impact of different upstream processing strategies for microbial production of the fragment antigen-binding (Fab) ranibizumab using Escherichia coli. Four bioreactor operation strategies were compared: fed-batch (FB), repetitive fed-batch (RFB), Chemostat cultivation, and a cascaded continuous setup.

The purpose of the dataset is to provide the underlying experimental and calculated data used for the sustainability assessment presented in the publication. The assessment combines process-based green metrics, namely process mass intensity (PMI), manufacturing mass intensity (MMI), and energetic footprint (EF), with a cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment (LCA). The LCA considers global warming potential (GWP) and water consumption footprint (WF).

Material consumption data were derived from the experimentally performed laboratory-scale cultivation processes and associated upstream unit operations. Electrical energy consumption of laboratory equipment was experimentally monitored where applicable. Additional energy demands, including purified-water production and conditioning as well as scale-dependent aeration and stirring scenarios, were calculated using literature data and process assumptions. LCA calculations were performed using SimaPro 9.6.0.1 with the ecoinvent 3.10 database and the ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint (H) impact assessment method. The functional unit of the sustainability assessment was 1 g of produced Fab.

Sensitivity and scenario analyses include variations in product titer (±20%), electricity supply mix, and scale-dependent stirring energy demand.

Technical details

The dataset consists of three Microsoft Excel workbooks:

PMI_MMI_data.xlsx contains the material input data and calculations used to determine PMI and MMI for the four upstream processing configurations. Data are provided by material category and unit operation, together with the corresponding product-normalized results and sensitivity calculations.

Energy_data.xlsx contains experimentally measured electrical energy data and calculated energy demands used to determine the energetic footprint (EF). Separate worksheets contain data for sterilization-in-place (SIP), pre-culture/incubation, bioreactor operation, centrifugation, purified-water production and conditioning, and aeration/stirring calculations. The summary_data worksheet combines these contributions and reports absolute and product-specific energy demands for the four process configurations.

LCA_data.xlsx contains the resulting life-cycle-assessment data for global warming potential and water consumption footprint, including contributions from individual process and material categories. The workbook additionally contains the data used for the scenario and sensitivity analyses.

The files can be opened with Microsoft Excel or compatible spreadsheet software. No specialized software is required to inspect the deposited data. Reproduction of the original LCA modelling from the underlying life-cycle inventory databases requires access to SimaPro and the corresponding ecoinvent database.

Further details

The four process configurations are abbreviated as FB (fed-batch), RFB (repetitive fed-batch), Chemostat, and Cascaded setup. Additional abbreviations used throughout the dataset include PMI (process mass intensity), MMI (manufacturing mass intensity), EF (energetic footprint), GWP (global warming potential), WF (water consumption footprint), SIP (sterilization-in-place), CIP (cleaning-in-place), PW (purified water), and Fab (fragment antigen-binding).

The system boundaries, process assumptions, experimental procedures, calculation methodology, and interpretation of the data are described in detail in the associated publication. The deposited spreadsheets contain both primary experimental measurements and derived/calculated values.

titles: Decision Neutrality of Forecast Revisions in Microgrids with Photovoltaics and Battery Storage - Supplementary Material
descriptions:
This dataset is the supplementary material for the manuscript "Decision Neutrality of Forecast Revisions in Microgrids with Photovoltaics and Battery Storage" by Yun Xing (Hohai University), submitted to Applied Sciences (MDPI). Version 1.0, 25 October 2026.

OverviewThe study asks when adopting a revised next-day forecast changes a battery dispatch decision, rather than only the predicted cost. It derives two checkable sufficient reset conditions under which old and revised forecasts produce next-day storage value functions that differ only by an additive constant. A fixed-input perturbation bound separates this local neutrality from realized rolling-policy performance. Five policies (FF, FS, SF, SS and DAY) are compared on 522 community-days from 270 measured households aggregated into nine synthetic communities, with three synthetic tariffs and two import regimes.

Key results- Freezing next-day forecasts is numerically neutral under unlimited imports across the tested tariffs.- Under a 30 kW import cap and time-of-use pricing, retaining midnight targets (DAY) lowers total operating cost by 3.105% relative to full updating (FF). Lower unmet-demand penalties account for 88.3% of the reduction; the import-bill reduction is 0.588%.- Freezing both forecasts while replanning (SS) costs 0.054% more than FF under the same six-hour replanning schedule, separating forecast adoption from target retention.- Under the same cap and tariff, freezing only the next-day forecast (FS) costs 0.188% more than FF.- Matched-calendar comparisons show that the magnitude of update effects depends on the controller scheme.

descriptions:

Grid 1 (120-Bin Fast-Proton Fokker-Planck Energy PDE): Solves the time-dependent advection-diffusion distribution f_f(E, t) across E in [15 keV, 900 keV]. Neutral beam protons are injected at the 597.4 keV (1.07 x 10^7 m/s) Sikora-Weller (2016) resonance peak (548 keV center-of-mass) and supported against collisional slowing-down by quasilinear radiofrequency (RF) alpha channeling locked to the fundamental proton / second-harmonic alpha cyclotron resonance (1 * Omega_p = 2 * Omega_alpha). Relativistic and Doppler resonance windowing naturally bounds fast-proton acceleration below 640 keV, preventing unphysical beam runaway while sustaining a hybrid fast-ion and thermal-ion burn (Kolmes, Ochs, & Fisch, 2022-2024).




Grid 2 (200-Node Rosenbluth Velocity-Space Drag & 2.5 Hz Breathing-Lung Thermal Separation): By the Rosenbluth-MacDonald-Judd (1957) Fokker-Planck shell theorem, net dynamical friction on a 597.4 keV proton is exerted exclusively by slow electrons with velocities v_e <= v_p, corresponding to a kinetic energy cutoff of E_e <= (m_e / m_p) * E_p = 325.4 eV (representing only 0.039% of a 50 keV Maxwellian electron bulk). MALT-OMEGA utilizes a synchronized 2.5 Hz electrostatic capacitor end-plug and ECH/laser thermal barrier cycle ("Breathing Lung") to selectively evacuate this sub-325.4 eV electron pocket while flushing cooled He-4 alpha ash (< 0.88% steady-state concentration; Ochs, Kolmes, & Fisch, 2025). The solver explicitly penalizes net electrical output by subtracting the continuous recirculating power required to maintain the depleted slow-electron cavity against electron-electron collisional refill (Physics of Plasmas 32, 012101, 2025).




Grid 3 (100-Node Radial Centrifugal-Ambipolar Stratification & 10-Pole Decapole Boundary): Solves the coupled Poisson-Boltzmann-centrifugal quasineutrality equations for rotating multi-species mirror plasmas (Kolmes, Ochs, & Fisch, Physical Review Letters 136, 085102, 2026). Azimuthal E x B rotation concentrates heavy 11B(5+) ions into an outer radial reaction shell (+34.2% effective target density across 0.50 <= r/a <= 0.92), while the resulting ambipolar electric field pushes thermal background protons inward ("inverted centrifugal confinement"), reducing orbit-averaged electron drag density along the fast-proton path to 82% of the bulk average. All Bremsstrahlung X-ray power is routed through a 60-node transient heat conduction solver modeling the 4-layer first wall (flowing liquid FLiBe curtain, SiC manifold, BN:H / HfO2 dielectric thermal barrier, and cascaded SiGe thermoelectric / sCO2 recovery loop operating at 42% thermal efficiency below the 450 C hot-junction limit and 2.80 MW/m^2 flux ceiling). Charged plasma exhaust exits through an Arefiev-Breizman (2008) supersonic ambipolar magnetic nozzle—which converts electron thermal pressure into directed axial ion kinetic energy—directly into a Rax, Kolmes, & Fisch (PRX Energy 4, 013007, 2025) gridless adiabatic grad-B and curvature drift Direct Energy Converter operating at 81% electrical recovery efficiency without inline grid sputtering.

To prevent high-beta diamagnetic drift from detuning the 1 * Omega_p = 2 * Omega_alpha cyclotron resonance lock (B_int = B_ext * sqrt(1 - beta) at design beta = 0.360), MALT-OMEGA pairs its primary high-temperature superconducting REBCO coils with an active low-inductance coated copper trimming coil (dB_Cu limited to +/- 2.00 T) and demand-throttled neutral beam injection. This mathematically bounds the compact 4.50 m^3 vessel to the 5.00 T - 8.275 T commercial window, while proving that utility-scale (> 100 MWe) ignited cores above 8.35 T simply require scaling the first-wall surface area from 16.0 m^2 to ~32.0 m^2.
